chunks: Rijal al-Kashshi: Hamdan ibn Ahmad, from Muawiya ibn Hukaym, from Abu Dawud al-Mustariq who said:

I was leading Abu Basir in one of the funeral processions of our companions when I said to him: 'There is Zurara in the procession.' He said to me: 'Take me to him.' So I took him to him. He said: 'Peace be upon you, O Abu al-Hasan.' Zurara returned the greeting to him and said to him: 'If I had known that this was of your own volition, I would have preceded you in it.' So Abu Basir said to him: 'I have been ordered to do this.'

key_terms.أَبُو بَصِير: Abu Basir, a companion known for being blind
key_terms.زُرَارَة: Zurara ibn A'yan, a prominent companion and narrator

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of Abu Basir's response to Zurara regarding the greeting in the funeral procession?
ai.summary: This anecdote from Rijal al-Kashshi illustrates the high status of Zurara among the companions, as Abu Basir’s deliberate greeting—citing a specific command—underscores the importance of initiating salutations with the learned. It highlights the scholarly etiquette (adab) within the Shia community, where greetings were not merely social pleasantries but acts of respect tied to religious instruction and hierarchical recognition.
